17510:
"Worried sick" means to be so deeply and intensely worried about something that the worry starts to feel like a physical illness. In other words, you are not just a little nervous or mildly concerned — you are worried to the maximum possible level, to the point where your body itself feels the impact.

Think of it this way: normal worry sits in your mind. But when you are worried sick, that worry has spread from your mind into your whole body — your stomach churns, your hands tremble, you can't eat, you can't sleep, and you feel genuinely unwell.

The word "sick" here does not mean you have a cold or a fever. It means the worry is so overwhelming and heavy that it mimics the feeling of being ill.
Breaking It Down Word by Word

• Worried = feeling anxious or uneasy about something that might go wrong.
  • Sick = feeling physically unwell, like your body is suffering.

Put together: "worried sick" = your worry has become so extreme that it has made your body feel sick.
The Core Idea: Worry as a Physical Experience

This expression is built on a very real human truth — that powerful emotions don't stay locked inside your head. They spill into your body. If you've ever felt your stomach drop when you received bad news, or felt your heart race before something scary, you already understand this connection between mind and body.

"Worried sick" captures that exact idea. It is the recognition that too much worry can feel as bad as a physical illness — nausea, headaches, loss of appetite, sleeplessness, a tight chest. The person using this phrase is saying: "My worry has gone beyond a thought. It has become something I feel in my whole body."
Is It Literal or Figurative?

This is an important question. The answer is: both, depending on the situation.

  • Figuratively (most common use): People use "worried sick" as a strong, expressive way of saying they are extremely worried. They don't literally have a fever or vomiting — they're just using powerful language to show how deeply concerned they are. This is called a hyperbole — a deliberate exaggeration used for emotional effect.
  • Literally (less common but real): Sometimes, extreme worry genuinely does make people physically ill. Anxiety is well-known to cause stomach pain, nausea, headaches, and more. In those cases, a person saying they are "worried sick" is being completely literal — the worry has actually made their body unwell.

Most of the time when someone says it, they mean it figuratively as an intensifier, but the emotional truth behind it is always real.
How Is It Used in a Sentence?

"Worried sick" is most commonly used in two patterns:

Pattern 1: "be worried sick"

"I was worried sick when you didn't call me back."
"She's been worried sick about her exam results."
"We were worried sick all night until we heard you were safe."

Pattern 2: "worry someone sick"

"You worried me sick by disappearing without telling anyone!"
"Don't worry your parents sick — just send a quick message."

In Pattern 1, the subject feels the worry.
In Pattern 2, the subject causes the worry in another person.
Who Uses This Expression?

This phrase is commonly used:

  • By parents talking about their children ("I was worried sick when you came home late").
  • By partners or spouses expressing concern for each other.
  • By friends who were anxious about someone's safety or wellbeing.
  • In everyday casual conversation — it is not formal language. You would not typically use it in a business report or an academic essay, but it is perfectly natural in spoken English and informal writing.

It is used across American English, British English, and most other varieties of English worldwide.
The Emotional Tone of the Phrase

When someone says "worried sick," they are not just giving you information — they are also expressing a strong emotional message. That message is usually one of:

  1. Deep love or care — "I care about you so much that your absence made me feel ill."
  2. Relief mixed with residual anxiety — often said after the stressful event has passed.
  3. A gentle reproach — a soft way of saying, "You caused me a lot of pain by doing that."

For example: "Where were you? I've been worried sick!" — This tells you the speaker loves or cares deeply about the listener, and that their absence caused genuine anguish.
Related Expressions You Should Know

Understanding "worried sick" becomes even richer when you see it alongside similar phrases:

  • "Worried to death" — Same meaning. Extreme worry, using "death" instead of "sick" as the intensifier. Slightly more dramatic in tone.
  • "Sick with worry" — This is the reversed form of the same idea ("sick with worry" vs. "worried sick"). Both mean exactly the same thing.
  • "On edge" — Feeling tense and anxious, but milder than worried sick.
  • "Beside oneself with worry" — To be so overwhelmed by worry that you feel almost out of control of yourself. Very similar intensity to "worried sick."
  • "A bundle of nerves" — Being extremely anxious and tense.

Among these, "worried sick" and "sick with worry" are direct twins — same meaning, just reversed in word order.
A Common Mistake to Avoid

Because the phrase contains the word "sick," some learners think it means someone is actually ill with a disease, and that they are also worried about something separately. That is not what it means. The sickness IS the worry — or rather, the worry is so intense it creates the feeling of sickness. There is only one event happening, not two.

❌ Wrong interpretation: "She is sick in bed AND she is worried."
✅ Correct interpretation: "She is so worried that she feels physically sick."
A Quick Memory Trick

If you ever forget the meaning, remember this image:

Picture someone pacing back and forth, unable to eat, unable to sleep, clutching their stomach — all because they're waiting for news about someone they love. They don't have a disease. But they feel like they do, because their worry is that powerful.

That is what "worried sick" looks like.
Summary in One Sentence

"Worried sick" means to be so intensely and deeply worried about something or someone that the worry feels like a physical illness — it is one of the strongest ways in the English language to express extreme anxiety and concern.
17511:
To worship means to show the highest possible level of devotion, reverence, and honor toward someone or something — to place them so far above yourself that your whole being turns toward them in submission, admiration, and love.

It is not ordinary respect. It is not even strong admiration. Worship sits at the very top of the scale of how much a person can honor something. When you worship, you are essentially saying: "You are so far above me that I surrender myself before you."
The Two Main Ways It Is Used

1. The religious sense (the original and most common meaning)

This is when a person worships a god, a deity, or a sacred being. In this sense, to worship means to perform acts of devotion that express your complete submission to and glorification of that being. These acts include prayer, singing hymns, kneeling, making offerings, chanting, performing rituals, and so on.

The key thing to understand here is that religious worship is not just a feeling — it is expressed outwardly. When someone worships God, they are not just privately thinking, "God is great." They are actively doing something to honor God — going to a temple, a church, or a mosque; reciting prayers; participating in ceremonies.

The feeling behind all of this is a mix of awe (the sense that this being is infinitely great and beyond your comprehension), love (a deep, devoted attachment), gratitude (for what this being has given you), and humility (the recognition that you are small in comparison).

Examples:

  • "Thousands gathered to worship at the temple during the festival."
  • "She worships every morning before sunrise."
  • "Different cultures worship different gods."

2. The non-religious or everyday sense

Outside of religion, you can also use "worship" to describe how intensely a person admires or loves another person or thing — so intensely that it resembles religious devotion.

When you say someone worships another person, you mean their admiration has gone beyond the normal level. It has become almost blind, total, and unconditional. They see this person as nearly perfect and place them on a very high pedestal.

This can apply to people, things, or even abstract concepts like money, fame, or success.

Examples:

  • "He worships his older brother — he wants to do everything exactly like him."
  • "She practically worships her favorite author."
  • "Some people worship money above everything else."
  • "The fans worship the singer as if she were a goddess."
How Worship Differs from Similar Words

This is important for understanding exactly where worship sits.

  • Respect — you think well of someone and treat them with dignity. It is calm and measured.
  • Admire — you look up to someone and feel positively about their qualities or achievements.
  • Adore — you love someone warmly and deeply. There is tenderness and affection in it.
  • Revere — you hold someone in very deep respect mixed with awe. This is stronger than admire or adore, but it is mostly a feeling.
  • Worship — this is the most extreme. It includes reverence, adoration, and love, but adds the element of devotion in action and a sense of the worshipper being beneath the one being worshipped. The worshipper orients their whole self toward that person or being.

Think of it as a ladder:
Respect → Admire → Adore → Revere → Worship

Worship is at the very top. It is total and consuming.
The Idea of Submission Within Worship

One thing that makes "worship" a very specific word is the quiet but important element of submission in it. When you worship something, you are not standing beside it as an equal. You are, in some sense, bowing before it.

This is obvious in religious worship — people literally bow, kneel, or prostrate themselves. But even in everyday use, when you say someone "worships" another person, you are implying that they have given up some of their own independence of thought. They place that person so high that they can barely question or criticize them.

This is why "worship" can sometimes carry a slightly critical tone in everyday use — suggesting that the admiration has become excessive or blind.
A Few Useful Phrases and Patterns

"Worship the ground someone walks on" — This is an idiom meaning you have such total admiration for a person that you respect even the ground beneath their feet. It suggests love or admiration that is almost embarrassingly extreme.

  • "He worships the ground she walks on."

"Worship at the altar of something" — This is a metaphorical phrase used to say that someone is completely devoted to something, treating it like a religion.

  • "He worships at the altar of ambition — nothing else matters to him."
  • "This culture worships at the altar of celebrity."

"Blind worship" — Devotion or admiration that ignores faults and refuses to think critically.

  • "Blind worship of any leader is dangerous."
The Emotional Texture of the Word

If you want to truly feel the word, imagine the experience of standing before something so vast, so beautiful, or so powerful that you feel completely small — and yet you are drawn to it, not in fear, but in love and awe. You want to be near it. You want to honor it. You want to give yourself to it. That feeling, combined with the action of expressing it, is worship.

It is intimate and grand at the same time. It is both a private inner state and something that naturally wants to be expressed outward.

To worship (verb) is to show the highest form of devotion, reverence, and honor — through acts, rituals, and heartfelt surrender — toward a god in the religious sense, or toward a person or thing you admire so completely that it resembles religious devotion in everyday life. It goes beyond respect or admiration; it involves awe, love, humility, and active expression, with the worshipper feeling subordinate to whatever or whoever is being worshipped.
17512: Most people know "worst" as an adjective — "That was the worst movie ever." But "worst" can also work as a verb, and that's what we're focusing on here.

To worst someone means to defeat them, to get the better of them in a competition, fight, debate, or any kind of contest.

When you worst someone, you don't just beat them — you overcome them decisively. The person who is worsted is the clear loser; the person doing the worsting is the clear winner.

Think of it as a more formal, literary way of saying "beat" or "defeat" — but specifically in a head-to-head contest where one side comes out on top and the other is clearly overcome.

FormExample
Baseworst
Past tenseworsted
Past participleworsted
Present participleworsting

(You'll see "worsted" most often, since this verb usually appears in the past tense.)
"Worst" as a verb is a transitive verb — it always needs an object. That means you worst someone; you can't just "worst" on its own. There must always be a person or group that gets defeated.

1. "The veteran boxer worsted his younger opponent in just two rounds."
→ The veteran boxer decisively defeated his opponent. The opponent was clearly overcome.

2. "Despite her nervousness, she worsted every other candidate in the interview process."
→ She outperformed and beat all the other candidates.

3. "The small army managed to worst their far more powerful enemy through clever strategy."
→ Despite being at a disadvantage, they defeated the enemy.

4. "He thought he could win the argument, but she worsted him with her clear evidence."
→ She got the better of him in the argument; he couldn't counter her.

5. "The defending champion was worsted for the first time in five years."
→ (Passive form.) The champion was defeated — someone got the better of him/her.

Notice how the passive form — "was worsted" — shifts the focus to the person who lost, rather than who won. This is common.
The feel of the word — when and why people use it

"Worst" as a verb is formal and literary. You won't hear it in casual conversation. People don't say "I worsted my brother at chess last night." Instead, they'd say "I beat my brother at chess."

You're much more likely to encounter "worsted" (the past tense) in:

  • Novels, especially older or classic literature
  • Formal writing
  • Journalism or commentary about competitions, battles, debates, legal disputes

The word carries a slightly grand, elevated tone. When a writer chooses "worsted" instead of "defeated," they often want to emphasize the completeness of the defeat — that the loser was truly overcome, not just narrowly beaten.

There is a type of smooth wool yarn and fabric also called worsted (as in "a worsted suit"). This is a completely different word that just happens to be spelled and pronounced the same as the past tense of the verb "to worst."

The context always makes it clear which one is meant:

  • "He was worsted in the battle." → verb; he was defeated.
  • "She wore a grey worsted jacket." → fabric; a type of smooth wool.
The core idea — in one sentence

To worst someone = to defeat or overcome them completely in any kind of contest, competition, or struggle.

That's the heart of it. The rest — the formal tone, the passive construction, the literary context — all flows naturally from that single meaning once you've understood it.
17513:
Worthless means having no value, no use, or no good qualities whatsoever.

If something is worthless, it gives you nothing — no benefit, no help, no monetary value, nothing of importance. It is the complete absence of worth.

To understand it fully, start with the word "worth." Worth means the value or usefulness something has. A gold coin has worth because you can exchange it for things. A good knife has worth because it cuts. A trustworthy friend has worth because they are reliable and caring. Now add "-less" — a suffix that means "without." So worthless = without worth. Zero value. Zero usefulness.

Worthless can describe things, people, efforts, and information. Each has its own flavour.

1. Objects and Things

When an object is worthless, it has no practical use and no monetary value.

"This cracked vase is worthless — nobody would buy it, and you can't even put water in it."

"After the company went bankrupt, its shares became worthless overnight."

A thing becomes worthless when it can no longer do what it was meant to do, or when no one finds any reason to want it.

2. People

This is the harshest use of the word. Calling a person worthless means you believe they have no good qualities, contribute nothing, and cannot be relied upon for anything.

"He was a worthless employee — he never finished a task and kept making excuses."

"Her father called her worthless, and those words stayed with her for years."

Important: Calling a person worthless is a serious insult. It is a sweeping, crushing judgment that denies them all human value. In real life, people rarely actually have zero value — this word, when applied to people, is almost always an exaggeration driven by anger or cruelty. Use it with care.

3. Efforts and Actions

An effort or action is worthless when it produces no result and leads nowhere.

"All our hard work was worthless — the entire project got cancelled."

"It's worthless arguing with him. He never listens."

Here, worthless is similar to saying the effort was pointless or futile — it achieved nothing.

4. Information, Advice, and Ideas

When information or advice is worthless, it is completely unhelpful — it does not solve your problem, it is irrelevant, or it is simply wrong.

"The map we were given was worthless — half the streets on it didn't exist."

"His advice was worthless. Following it only made things worse."

This is an important distinction.

Objective worthlessness means something has no value by any reasonable standard — not just in your opinion, but by any measure.

A counterfeit banknote is objectively worthless as money. No store will accept it. Its "value" is an illusion.

Subjective worthlessness means you find something worthless, though others might not.

"I find reality TV completely worthless."

Here, you are expressing a personal judgment. Someone else might love reality TV and find it very valuable for entertainment.

The word can carry both meanings, so context always matters. When someone says something is worthless, ask yourself: is this a fact, or an opinion?

The word takes on a deep emotional meaning when someone says they feel worthless.

"After losing his job and his relationship in the same month, he felt completely worthless."

To feel worthless means to feel as though you have no value as a person — that you matter to no one, that nothing you do makes a difference, that the world would be no different without you. It is one of the most painful emotional states a person can experience, and it is closely associated with depression and low self-esteem.

This use of the word is not about money or usefulness — it is about a person's sense of their own importance and place in the world.

Worthlessness is not always total. The word can be intensified or softened.

  • Completely / totally / utterly worthless — zero value, in the strongest possible terms.

    "The warranty was utterly worthless — they refused every single claim."

  • Practically worthless — almost no value, though perhaps not quite zero.

    "By the time we arrived, the medicine was practically worthless — it had expired months ago."

  • Worthless for a specific purpose — has no value in a particular context, though it might have value elsewhere.

    "A hammer is worthless for cutting wood, but perfect for driving nails."

The tone of worthless ranges from neutral to deeply hurtful, depending on what it describes.

  • Applied to objects or things: Usually neutral and factual. No emotional weight.

    "The old printer is worthless now — it doesn't support modern software."

  • Applied to efforts or information: Mildly negative. Can sound dismissive or disappointed.

    "That meeting was worthless. We decided nothing."

  • Applied to people: Very harsh and emotionally loaded. Avoid using this casually.

    "You're worthless." — This is a deeply insulting and hurtful statement.

The key rule: the more personal the target, the more emotionally destructive the word becomes.
Similar Words — and How They Differ

Understanding how worthless compares to related words will sharpen your grasp of it.

Useless — cannot perform its function. Focuses on the inability to do something.

"A pen with no ink is useless." (It can't write.)
"Useless" is often gentler than "worthless" and rarely implies total absence of value.

Valueless — has no monetary or material value. More formal and neutral.

"The land was valueless because it flooded every year."

Pointless — has no purpose or meaning. Focuses on the why, not the what.

"It's pointless to water dead plants." (There's no reason to do it.)

Futile — refers to efforts that are doomed to fail.

"It was futile to resist." (No matter what you do, it won't work.)

Good-for-nothing — applied only to people; informal and quite rude. Suggests the person is lazy and unreliable.

"He's a good-for-nothing layabout."

Meaningless — has no meaning or significance. Focuses on a lack of sense or purpose, not necessarily value.

"To him, life felt meaningless." (Not that he had no value, but that nothing seemed to matter.)

The main thing that sets worthless apart is its completeness — it suggests a total absence of value, more sweeping than most of these alternatives.

If something is not worthless, it is:

  • Valuable — has significant worth or usefulness
  • Precious — of great value, often emotionally or materially
  • Priceless — so valuable it cannot be measured in money
  • Useful — can be used effectively for a purpose
  • Beneficial — produces a good result or improvement
  • Worthwhile — worth the time, effort, or cost spent on it
A Few More Examples to Cement It

"The contract was written so vaguely that it was worthless in court — it couldn't protect anyone."

"She spent three hours looking for her lost keys, and in the end the locksmith's advice was worthless — he didn't even know the model."

"Growing up in an abusive home, she was told she was worthless. It took years of therapy to unlearn that lie."

"Gold became worthless in that fictional world because everyone had too much of it."

"A parachute that doesn't open is worse than worthless — it's dangerous."

Worthless = having absolutely no value, use, or good qualities — whether you're talking about an object, a person, an effort, or a piece of information.

The word is complete and final. It leaves nothing. Where there is worth, there is reason to care about something. Where there is worthlessness, there is not.
17514:
Worthy means: having enough genuine value, quality, or merit to deserve something.

Think of it like a bar or a standard. Something is "worthy" when it clears that bar — when its qualities are good enough to justify the recognition, respect, or reward being considered.
The Two Main Ways It's Used

1. Worthy of something

This is the most common pattern: [person or thing] is worthy of [what they deserve].

  • "She is worthy of your trust." → Her character genuinely earns your trust.
  • "This cause is worthy of support." → This cause has real value; it deserves to be supported.
  • "He proved himself worthy of the award." → He earned it; he met the standard it demands.
  • "Not every idea is worthy of consideration." → Some ideas are weak enough to safely ignore.

The word "of" is the signal here. Something is worthy of praise, attention, respect, admiration, trust, etc.

2. Worthy before a noun (or on its own)

Here, it simply means having real merit; genuinely good or admirable.

  • "a worthy opponent" → an opponent who is genuinely capable and deserves to be taken seriously
  • "a worthy cause" → a cause that is genuinely valuable, not trivial
  • "a worthy goal" → a goal that is meaningful and worth working toward
  • "a worthy effort" → an effort that is genuinely good and deserves recognition
  • "He is a worthy successor." → He is good enough to follow in someone's footsteps with honor.

The key idea inside "worthy" is that the merit is real and earned, not just claimed or apparent. When you call something worthy, you're saying it has actually cleared the bar — it genuinely deserves what it's being considered for.

This is why "worthy" often carries a tone of honest evaluation and judgment. It's a word with weight to it. It's not casual flattery. It implies you've measured something against a real standard and found it to be enough.

"Worthy" has a slightly formal, dignified tone. It's the kind of word you'd hear in a serious conversation, a speech, or writing — not in quick everyday chat where you'd just say "deserving" instead.

Because of this elevated tone, "worthy" is also often used in solemn or noble contexts:

  • "No one is truly worthy of such an honor." (expressing humility)
  • "He was found worthy of knighthood."
  • "She finally had a worthy challenge before her."

Just as "worthy" means meeting the standard, saying someone is not worthy (or unworthy) means they fall below it — they haven't earned what they seek, or they don't have the qualities needed.

  • "He was unworthy of her loyalty." → He didn't deserve it; his actions or character failed to earn it.
  • "I am not worthy of this praise." → A humble way of saying the praise is too generous for what you've done.

This is also why "worthy" can sometimes feel like a slight when used in reverse. Calling someone's idea "not worthy of a response" is a sharp dismissal.

One of the most useful things about this word is how it combines with other words to create compound adjectives. The suffix -worthy means "deserving of" or "fit for."

  • trustworthy → worthy of trust (you can rely on this person)
  • noteworthy → worthy of note (deserving your attention; remarkable)
  • praiseworthy → worthy of praise (deserving admiration)
  • blameworthy → worthy of blame (deserving to be held responsible)
  • creditworthy → worthy of credit (a lender can trust you to repay a loan)
  • newsworthy → worthy of news coverage (important or interesting enough to report)
  • roadworthy → fit to be on the road (a vehicle that's safe to drive)
  • seaworthy → fit for the sea (a ship strong enough to sail safely)
  • airworthy → fit to fly (an aircraft that's safe to operate)

Notice that some (trustworthy, praiseworthy) lean on "deserving of," while others (roadworthy, seaworthy) lean more on "fit for" or "capable of handling." Both shades come from the same word.

Worthy vs. Deserving
These are very close. "Deserving" is the more casual, everyday word. "Worthy" is a touch more formal and implies the person or thing has intrinsic qualities — something deep about their nature or character — that justifies the recognition. You can say "he's deserving of a raise" in a casual conversation; "he is worthy of respect" sounds more considered and weighty.

Worthy vs. Admirable
"Admirable" specifically means deserving admiration. "Worthy" is broader — something can be worthy of respect, trust, attention, praise, or many other things, not just admiration.

Worthy vs. Meritorious
"Meritorious" is more formal and usually applies to specific actions or achievements (a meritorious service award). "Worthy" applies to people, things, causes, and ideas more broadly.

Whenever you see or use "worthy," ask: What standard is being met here? The word always implies that something has cleared a bar — that its qualities, character, or merit genuinely justify the respect, recognition, or consideration being offered. It's a word of honest, earned approval. When something is worthy, it has actually proven itself.
17515: Before anything else, be careful here. The word "wound" in this idiom is not pronounced like the word "wound" meaning an injury (as in a cut on your skin). In this idiom, it rhymes with "found," "sound," and "round." Say it like: "WOWND up." This trips up many learners, so keep it in mind.
The Core Idea Behind the Idiom

To truly understand "wound up," picture an old-fashioned clock or a music box. To make it work, you insert a key and turn it round and round, tightening a metal spring inside. The more you turn the key, the tighter the spring gets. When it is fully tightened, the spring is full of stored energy — it is tense, coiled, and ready to release. This is called being "wound up."

This physical image is the heart of the idiom. Whether it describes a person's emotions, the end of a situation, or a joke being played on someone, the idea of something being "coiled, brought to a point, or brought to a conclusion" runs through every meaning.

"Wound up" is versatile. It works in four distinct ways, and each one is important.

Meaning 1 — Feeling Anxious, Tense, or Stressed

This is the most common everyday meaning. When a person is described as "wound up," it means they are nervous, tense, stressed, or worked up about something — just like that tightly coiled spring.

Examples:

  • "She was so wound up before the job interview that she couldn't sleep."
  • "Stop being so wound up — it's just a game, relax!"
  • "He gets easily wound up when people are late."

You can make it stronger by saying "all wound up" — this emphasizes how deeply tense the person is.

  • "The kids were all wound up on Christmas Eve and refused to go to bed."

The feeling it describes: Think of that tight, buzzing, restless energy you feel when you are nervous about something, or when something is irritating you and you cannot calm down. Your mind is racing, your body is tense, and you feel like you cannot switch off. That is being "wound up."

Meaning 2 — To Eventually End Up in a Situation (Often Unexpectedly)

Here, "wound up" is used as a phrasal verb (to wind up) meaning to finally arrive at a result, place, or situation — often one that was not planned or expected. Think of a path that twists and turns and eventually leads you somewhere. You "wind up" wherever that path ends.

Examples:

  • "We took a wrong turn and wound up on the other side of the city."
  • "He never studied and wound up failing all his exams."
  • "I only meant to watch one episode, but I wound up watching the whole season."
  • "She moved to Paris for six months and wound up staying for six years."

The key feeling of this meaning: There is usually a sense of something happening gradually, accidentally, or as a consequence of events. You did not necessarily plan to be in that situation — you just found yourself there. It often carries a slight tone of surprise or irony.

A very natural way to use it: "How did you wind up becoming a chef?" — meaning, how did you end up in that career, what path led you there?

Meaning 3 — To Finish or Bring Something to a Close

In this meaning, "wind up" means to conclude, wrap up, or end something — like the final turns of a key before the spring is fully coiled and the winding is done.

Examples:

  • "Let's wind up this meeting — we've covered everything."
  • "She wound up her speech with a funny story."
  • "The company decided to wind up its operations in Europe."
  • "It's getting late, so let's wind things up for today."

The key feeling of this meaning: It signals that something is being brought to a deliberate, orderly close. It is often used in professional or formal contexts — meetings, speeches, projects, businesses. It is a polite and natural way to signal an ending.

Meaning 4 — To Tease, Trick, or Mess With Someone (Mainly British English)

This meaning is very popular in British and Australian English and might confuse you if you are not aware of it. To "wind someone up" means to deliberately tease them, trick them into believing something false, or intentionally irritate them — for fun or out of mischief.

Examples:

  • "Are you winding me up? There's no way that actually happened!"
  • "He told me I failed the test, but he was just winding me up."
  • "My brother loves winding me up by hiding my things."
  • "Don't let him wind you up — he does it to everyone."

The noun form is a "wind-up" — meaning the act of teasing or a joke played on someone.

  • "Relax, it was just a wind-up!"

The key feeling of this meaning: Imagine someone turning a key in your back — slowly getting a reaction out of you. They are deliberately pushing your buttons, either as a harmless joke or to get under your skin. If someone says "you're being wound up," it means you are being teased and perhaps falling for it.
How to Know Which Meaning is Being Used

Since "wound up" has multiple meanings, context is your guide. Here is how to figure it out quickly:

If it describes a person's emotional state → They are anxious or tense.
(He is wound up about the presentation.)

If it follows a story of events leading somewhere → Someone ended up in a situation.
(She wound up losing everything.)

If someone is ending a task or event → Something is being concluded.
(Let's wind up the discussion.)

If it involves teasing or someone reacting to a prank → Someone is being messed with. (British/Australian context)
(He was winding her up the whole time.)
Common Phrases and Patterns to Remember

• "All wound up" — very tense or agitated (Don't get all wound up about it.)
  • "Wound up in" — ended up in a place or situation (They wound up in serious trouble.)
  • "Wind things up" — to wrap up what you are doing (Let's wind things up here.)
  • "Wind up doing something" — to eventually do something, often unintentionally (I wound up doing all the work myself.)
  • "Are you winding me up?" — British expression of disbelief, meaning "Are you joking?" or "Are you serious?"

"Wound up" comes from the image of a tightly coiled spring and carries the idea of tension, conclusion, and arrival. It can mean a person is emotionally tense, that someone ended up in a situation, that something is being brought to a close, or (in British English) that someone is being teased or mocked. Once you know which meaning fits the context, the idiom becomes very natural and easy to use.
17516: A wraith is a ghost — but not just any ghost. It's a very specific kind: a pale, shadowy, barely-visible spirit of a dead person. Think of it as the ghostly outline of a human being, thin and transparent, drifting silently like mist or smoke. It has a shape, but no real substance. You can almost see through it.
What Makes a Wraith Different from a Regular Ghost

The word "ghost" is broad and general. A wraith is more specific. Here's what sets it apart:

1. It is associated with death omens.
In old folklore (especially Scottish and Northern English tradition), a wraith wasn't always the spirit of someone already dead. It was sometimes the ghostly double of a living person — and seeing someone's wraith was considered a terrifying sign that that person was about to die very soon. So if you saw what looked like your neighbour walking silently through a wall at midnight, that was his wraith, and it meant he was doomed.

2. It looks like a faded, hollowed-out human.
A wraith doesn't look cheerful or solid. It looks like all the life has been drained out of a person — pale, sunken, barely there. It's the ghost of a person reduced to almost nothing.

3. It carries a dark, threatening energy.
Wraiths are not neutral or harmless ghosts. They are unsettling. They are associated with suffering, death, and dark supernatural power. In modern fantasy (think Tolkien's Ringwraiths, also called the Nazgûl), wraiths are among the most feared and malevolent beings imaginable — once-human souls completely consumed and enslaved by evil, with no will or identity of their own left.

"Wraith" is also used outside the supernatural, as a figure of speech, to describe something that is:

  • Ghostly thin or insubstantial — "A wraith of smoke curled from the candle." Here, the smoke is so thin and wispy it resembles a wraith.
  • A pale shadow of what something once was — "After months of illness, he had become a wraith." This means the person had become so thin, pale, and hollow-looking that he resembled a ghost — barely recognizable as his former self.
  • A faint trace or remnant — "Only a wraith of her former confidence remained." Almost nothing left of it.

In all figurative uses, the core idea is the same: something drained of substance, life, or solidity.
How It Feels to Use the Word

"Wraith" is not a casual, everyday word. When writers and speakers use it, they are trying to evoke something eerie, foreboding, and otherworldly. The word itself sounds haunting — it fits naturally in dark, atmospheric writing. You wouldn't say "I saw a wraith at the supermarket" in a comic way; the word automatically adds weight and darkness to any sentence it enters.

• "The wraith drifted silently through the stone walls of the castle, visible for only a moment before vanishing."
  • "In the legend, seeing your own wraith meant your death was near."
  • "She stood at the edge of the fog — thin, silent, motionless — like a wraith."
  • "The wraith of his old ambition haunted him, a reminder of who he had once been."

AspectWhat to Remember

To remember "wraith" cleanly: it is a shadowy, insubstantial ghost — thin, pale, and associated with death, dark power, or the near-complete disappearance of something. It can be literal (a supernatural spirit) or figurative (a person or thing reduced to a ghost of itself). It always carries a dark, foreboding feeling. It is never cheerful, never ordinary, never light.
17517:
To understand wraithlike, you first need a clear picture of a wraith.

A wraith is a ghost — but not the cartoonish, friendly kind. It's the pale, thin, barely-there kind of ghost: a silent, drifting figure that seems to have almost no physical substance. It's the kind of spirit you'd see gliding through a dark corridor, more shadow than body, there and gone in an instant.

Wraithlike means: resembling a wraith. When you describe something — usually a person or a figure — as wraithlike, you are saying it has the qualities of that kind of ghost.

Wraithlike bundles together several qualities at once. Here's what it really points to:

1. Extreme paleness and thinness.
A wraithlike person is usually described as very pale (almost colourless, like skin drained of blood) and very thin — not just slim, but bony, almost skeletal. The body looks fragile, barely substantial, as if illness or suffering has worn it down to almost nothing.

2. A ghostly, barely-there presence.
Wraithlike suggests that a person or figure seems as though they are not fully of the physical world. They appear insubstantial — as if they might pass through a wall, or dissolve into the air. Even when they are clearly physically present, something about them feels unreal, like a shadow given the shape of a person.

3. Silent, drifting movement.
Things that are wraithlike often move in a quiet, gliding way — without sound, without weight. They don't stamp their feet or knock things over. They appear and disappear. They drift rather than walk.

4. An eerie, unsettling quality.
Wraithlike carries a feeling of unease. When you say someone looks or moves wraithlike, you're not saying they look elegant or delicate in a positive sense. There's something off about it — something that makes the observer feel a quiet sense of dread or discomfort.
What can be described as wraithlike?

Most commonly, you'll see wraithlike used to describe:

  • A person's appearance: Someone who is extremely gaunt, pale, and sickly. "After months of illness, she was a wraithlike figure — hollow cheeks, grey skin, eyes that seemed too large for her face."
  • A person's presence or manner: Someone who moves silently, appears suddenly without warning, and seems to leave no mark on a room. "He moved through the house in a wraithlike way, and you'd never know he had passed unless you caught the faint scent of him."
  • A figure seen in poor light or at a distance: A silhouette, a shape in fog or darkness that resembles a ghost. "A wraithlike shape drifted between the trees."
  • Anything that is thin, faint, and barely there: Occasionally, writers use it for non-human things, like smoke, mist, or a faded image — anything that is ghostly-thin and insubstantial.

This is an important part of the word that learners often miss.

Wraithlike is not a neutral word, and it is not a compliment in the conventional sense. It does not mean beautifully thin or gracefully pale. It means ghostly-thin, unsettlingly pale. It carries a suggestion of suffering, illness, lifelessness, or something supernatural and eerie. When you call someone wraithlike, you are evoking a kind of quiet horror or sadness — not admiration.

That said, in literature, it can be used admiringly when the writer wants to suggest something otherworldly or ethereal about a character — but even then, the eerie quality is always present.

Very strong. It is not a mild descriptor. You would not call someone wraithlike if they simply looked a bit pale or slightly thin. The word is reserved for people or things that look dramatically, strikingly, almost unnaturally ghost-like. It amplifies to the extreme.

To sharpen your understanding, here's what wraithlike is not:

  • It does not simply mean thin. A thin, healthy, well-rested person would never be called wraithlike.
  • It does not mean mysterious on its own. A person can be mysterious without being wraithlike.
  • It does not mean transparent in the literal sense (you can still see the person clearly).
  • It is not the same as ghost-like in a playful or costume-party sense. It has a genuinely eerie, slightly disturbing quality.
Register: when and where this word appears

Wraithlike is a literary and descriptive word. You will almost never hear it in casual everyday conversation. You'll find it in:

  • Novels (especially Gothic fiction, fantasy, or literary fiction)
  • Poetry
  • Descriptive prose and journalism when a writer wants a very vivid, atmospheric image

If you use it in writing, it immediately signals careful, stylish, literary language. It is a word that paints rather than merely describes.
A few sentences to cement it

• "The famine survivors were wraithlike figures, barely capable of standing."
  • "She moved through the corridors in a wraithlike silence, unseen until she was right beside you."
  • "The wraithlike shape of a man stood at the edge of the fog."
  • "Years of isolation had given him a wraithlike quality — pale, hollow-eyed, and oddly weightless in his movements."

Wraithlike means: having the appearance or qualities of a ghost — extremely pale, thin, insubstantial, eerily silent, and barely seeming to belong to the physical world. It is a strong, literary word that implies something unsettling, not merely delicate.
17518: To wrangle means to deal with something — or someone — that resists you. That resistance is the key. Whether you're arguing with a person, herding animals, fighting to get something you want, or wrestling with a difficult task, there is always friction, back-and-forth, and effort involved. Keep that image in mind — it ties all the meanings together.
Meaning 1: To Argue in a Heated, Prolonged Way

This is the most common meaning. When people wrangle, they aren't just having a quiet disagreement — they are arguing in a way that is noisy, stubborn, and drawn out, where neither side easily backs down.

"The politicians wrangled over the budget for weeks without reaching any agreement."

"The two business partners wrangled constantly about how the company should be run."

The word carries a slightly critical tone. Calling an argument "wrangling" often implies it is becoming tiresome, circular, or unproductive — like two people pulling on a rope from opposite ends and going nowhere.

Compare this to just saying "they argued." Arguing is neutral. Wrangling suggests it went on too long, got too heated, or was messier than it needed to be.

Common pairings:

  • "wrangle over something" — to argue about a specific issue
  • "wrangle with someone" — to be in a prolonged dispute with a person

"They wrangled over who would inherit the property."
"She wrangled with the insurance company for months before getting her money."
Meaning 2: To Herd or Round Up Animals (especially horses)

In ranching and farming — particularly in American English — wrangle means to gather animals (most often horses or cattle) and drive them where you want them to go.

"Every morning, the cowboy would wrangle the horses from the open field into the stable."

This is a physical act of controlling animals that don't simply follow orders. You have to chase, guide, and corral them — again, the idea of friction and effort is present.

This is why someone who manages and looks after horses on a film set or at a ranch is called a wrangler (also "horse wrangler"). You'll also hear "animal wrangler" used for people who handle animals on movie and TV productions.
Meaning 3: To Obtain Something Through Effort, Persistence, or Clever Maneuvering

In informal speech, wrangle means to get or secure something that wasn't easy to get — usually by being persistent, persuasive, or a bit clever. You didn't just receive it; you worked for it or found a smart way to get it.

"She managed to wrangle a table at the fully booked restaurant."
"He wrangled two extra weeks to finish the project."
"The journalist wrangled an interview with the reclusive billionaire."

Here the word has a slightly admiring or impressed tone — it suggests resourcefulness. The person didn't just ask politely and receive; they navigated something difficult.

Common pattern: "wrangled + his/her/their way into..." means to get into something through effort or cleverness.

"He wrangled his way into the exclusive conference even without an invitation."
Meaning 4: To Struggle With Something Difficult and Messy

Wrangle also describes the act of dealing with — wrestling with — a task that is complicated, disorganized, or resistant to being solved. This use is common in professional and technical contexts.

"The accountant spent three days wrangling the messy financial records into proper order."
"She's been wrangling with this software bug for hours."

You'll very commonly hear the phrase "data wrangling" — a technical term that refers to the process of cleaning, organizing, and transforming raw, messy data into a usable format. It's called wrangling because the data is chaotic and resists easy handling, just like an unruly herd of animals.

The tone here is of hard, unglamorous work — you're not elegantly solving a problem, you're getting your hands dirty fighting through something stubborn.
The One Thread That Connects Everything

Every single use of wrangle involves the same feeling: something is resisting you, and you are pushing through that resistance with effort and persistence.

  • In an argument → the other person resists you
  • In herding → the animals resist being moved
  • In obtaining something → the situation or person resists giving it to you
  • In tackling a difficult task → the problem itself resists being solved

That sense of struggle is always there.

Wrangle is slightly informal in tone. You would use it in everyday conversation, journalism, and casual writing — but you'd rarely find it in formal legal or academic prose.

It often carries a gentle negative or tired quality when used about arguments (suggesting the argument is a waste of energy), but a slightly impressed quality when used about obtaining something (suggesting cleverness and persistence).

Wrangle with someone / wrangle over something → argue heatedly and at length

Wrangle animals → herd and control livestock

Wrangle something → obtain it through effort, persistence, or cunning

Wrangle with a task / wrangle something into shape → struggle through something difficult and messy

One word, one underlying feeling: effort against resistance. Once you internalize that, every use of wrangle will feel completely natural.
17519: Wrangling has two distinct core meanings. Think of them as the "arguing" meaning and the "herding" meaning. Both are widely used, and once you understand them, you'll recognize the word everywhere.
Meaning 1: A prolonged, messy argument or dispute

This is the most common meaning in everyday English. When people engage in wrangling, they are not just having a quick disagreement — they are locked in a drawn-out, back-and-forth argument, often over something complicated, where no one wants to back down. It carries a sense of friction, stubbornness, and the feeling that things are going in circles rather than moving forward.

The key qualities of this kind of wrangling:

  • It goes on for a long time
  • It is heated and contentious
  • It is often frustrating and exhausting to watch or be part of
  • It rarely feels productive, even if it eventually leads to a conclusion
  • It often involves multiple rounds of disagreement, negotiation, and pushback

This meaning is especially common in political, legal, business, and organizational contexts — anywhere people need to reach an agreement but struggle to do so.

Examples:

  • "After months of wrangling, the two political parties finally agreed on a budget."
  • "The shareholders' meeting descended into wrangling over who should lead the company."
  • "There was intense legal wrangling before the case even went to trial."
  • "The wrangling between the two teams delayed the project by weeks."

Why use "wrangling" instead of just "argument" or "fight"?

"Argument" and "fight" can be short and sharp. Wrangling, by nature, is prolonged and messy. It suggests a process — a grinding back-and-forth — rather than a single explosive moment. If someone says "they had an argument," it might have lasted five minutes. If someone says "there was wrangling," you picture something that dragged on for days, weeks, or even months, with many people involved and no clean resolution in sight. It also sounds slightly undignified — the word itself has a rough, tangled quality to it that mirrors the experience it describes.
Meaning 2: The act of herding, rounding up, or managing animals (especially horses and cattle)

This is the older, more literal meaning. It comes from the world of cowboys and ranching. A person who rounds up, handles, and manages horses or cattle is called a wrangler. The act of doing that work is called wrangling.

Examples:

  • "Horse wrangling is a skill that takes years to learn."
  • "Cattle wrangling on the open range was the backbone of the American West."

You will see this meaning in contexts related to ranching, rodeos, Western history, and outdoor adventure tourism (where staff who manage horses for guests are called wranglers).
Meaning 3: The extended modern use — struggling to manage or control something difficult

Because wrangling (in both the argument sense and the herding sense) involves effort, difficulty, and messiness, English speakers have naturally extended the word to mean dealing with anything that is hard to control, organize, or manage.

This extended use is now extremely common, especially in professional and technical contexts.

Examples:

  • Data wrangling — In technology, this refers to the process of taking raw, messy, disorganized data and cleaning it, organizing it, and transforming it into a usable format. It is painstaking and unglamorous work, which is exactly why the word "wrangling" fits it so well.
  • Child wrangling — Informally, this describes the exhausting task of managing energetic, unpredictable children, especially in a group setting (like a birthday party or a classroom).
  • Wrangling volunteers — Managing a large group of volunteers who are hard to coordinate and keep on track.
  • "She spent the whole afternoon wrangling her children into their costumes for the school play."
  • "The event coordinator was busy wrangling all the vendors and making sure everyone showed up on time."

In all these cases, the idea is the same: you are dealing with something that resists easy control, requires significant effort, and demands patience.
The tone and feel of the word

"Wrangling" is not a neutral word. It carries a slightly negative or weary tone. When you use it, you are implicitly saying:

  • This was harder than it should have been
  • There was friction and resistance involved
  • Things felt messy and unruly

This makes it a very expressive and honest word. It does not prettify or sanitize the situation. Instead of saying "we had productive discussions," saying "there was a lot of wrangling" tells the listener that it was difficult, frustrating, and complicated.
Common collocations (words you will often see beside "wrangling")

• Political wrangling — arguments among politicians
  • Legal wrangling — disputes in a legal context, often drawn-out court battles or negotiations between lawyers
  • Budget wrangling — debates and disagreements over money and spending
  • Internal wrangling — conflict happening within an organization, party, or group
  • Data wrangling — the technical process of organizing messy data

Wrangling (as a noun) means one of these three things:

  1. A prolonged, messy, exhausting argument or dispute — the kind that drags on without easy resolution
  2. The act of herding and managing livestock, especially horses or cattle
  3. (By extension) The difficult, effortful process of managing, organizing, or controlling anything that is unruly or hard to handle

The word always carries the sense of struggle, effort, and friction — whether you are arguing with someone who won't budge, chasing cattle across a field, or trying to make sense of a chaotic spreadsheet.
